message:
ok so I'm trying to get my money life together lol. context: I'm 24, just started my first proper salaried job after two years of bar work, and for the first time ever I have a little bit of money that isn't already spoken for. a few things:

can you explain what an emergency fund is actually supposed to be for, like what counts as an emergency? and what's a good name for a savings pot in my banking app that'll actually stop me raiding it. also my friend keeps saying I should do a "no-spend month". give me three rules that would make one realistic and not miserable. and is a spreadsheet or an app better for tracking spending if I'm honestly kind of lazy? one-line answer is fine.

I've got $5,000 that I'm putting in a high-yield savings account at 4% a year, compounded monthly, and I'm leaving it completely alone for 3 years. I worked out I'll have $5,600 at the end (4% x 3 years = 12%, so $600 interest). is that right? what will it actually be?

last thing, rewrite this text to my landlord so it sounds less passive-aggressive: "As I have ALREADY mentioned twice, the bathroom fan is still broken." I don't want to start a war, I just want the fan fixed before winter.

thanks!! sorry this is so long, I've been putting all of this off for months and figured I'd just ask everything at once. my plan is to sit down sunday afternoon with a coffee and actually set all this up properly instead of just thinking about it, so whatever you send back is basically my to-do list for the weekend. (my parents are not money people at all, so I'm learning this from scratch and from tiktok, which is probably not ideal)
response:
You're doing this the right way. Here's everything, with a checklist at the end for Sunday.

## What an emergency fund is for

It's money set aside for **unexpected, necessary** costs, so a bad week doesn't turn into credit card debt. A good test is: *is it surprising, is it essential, and is it urgent?*

**Counts as an emergency:**
- Losing your job or a big cut in hours
- Medical or dental bills
- Urgent car repairs if you need the car for work
- A broken phone or laptop you need for work
- Last-minute travel for a family emergency
- An unexpected rent increase, or moving costs you didn't choose

**Doesn't count:**
- Sales, concerts, holidays or birthday gifts. These are predictable, so save for them separately.
- "I've had a rough week."

**How much:** a common target is **3–6 months of essential expenses** (rent, bills, food, transport). That can feel huge, so start with a mini-goal of **$1,000** or one month's expenses, then build up.

## Savings pot names that discourage raiding
- **"Future Me Is Counting On This"**
- **"Only If The Car Explodes"**
- **"Do Not Touch: Emergencies Only"**

Pick one that makes you hesitate before moving money out. If your bank allows it, keep the pot **out of view on your main screen**, or at a different bank, so it takes a deliberate effort to move money out.

## Three rules for a no-spend month that won't make you miserable
1. **Decide your essentials up front.** Rent, bills, groceries, transport and medication are allowed. The month only cuts *non-essential* spending, so you aren't skipping meals to "win."
2. **Give yourself one small treat allowance.** For example, $40 for the month, or one coffee out a week. A plan with no slack usually breaks by day 10.
3. **Replace, don't just remove.** Line up free things you'd enjoy: walks, library books, cooking with friends, free events. Unsubscribe from shop emails and delete shopping apps for the month.

## Spreadsheet or app?
**An app, if you're honest about being lazy.** It categorises spending automatically, while a spreadsheet only works if you update it.

## Your savings maths

Close, but slightly low. You've worked out **simple interest** (4% × 3 = 12% → $600). Compounding monthly means you also earn interest on your interest:

**$5,000 × (1 + 0.04/12)^36 ≈ $5,636.36**, about **$636 interest**, so roughly $36 more than your estimate.

Two things to know:
- **Savings rates usually change.** High-yield accounts are variable, so 4% today might be 3% or 5% next year. Treat $5,636 as a ballpark, not a promise.
- **Check whether the 4% is the APY.** Most US banks quote APY, which already includes compounding. If so, the figure is $5,000 × 1.04³ ≈ **$5,624**. Either way, you'll end up somewhere around $5,620–$5,640 if the rate holds.

(Interest on savings is usually taxable income. It's small at this level, but don't be surprised when the bank sends you a tax form.)

## The landlord text

> Hi [Name], just following up on the bathroom fan, which is still not working. I'd really like to get it sorted before winter so damp doesn't become an issue. Could you let me know when someone might be able to take a look? Happy to work around a time that suits. Thanks!

It's polite and specific, and mentioning damp gives the landlord a reason to act, since mould is their problem too. **Keep a copy of your messages** in case you ever need to show you reported it.

## A note on learning from TikTok

You're not starting behind. Asking these questions at 24 puts you ahead of a lot of people. Some advice on TikTok is great, but be wary of anyone promising fast returns or pushing a product. The boring basics (emergency fund, avoiding high-interest debt, saving automatically) do most of the work.

## Your Sunday checklist ☕
- [ ] Open or rename your emergency savings pot, and hide it from your main screen if you can
- [ ] Add up your essential monthly costs and set a first target (e.g. $1,000 or one month's essentials)
- [ ] Set up an **automatic transfer** to savings on payday, even if it's small
- [ ] Download a budgeting app and connect your accounts
- [ ] Check whether your 4% account rate is APY, and note it's variable
- [ ] Write your three no-spend-month rules and pick a start date
- [ ] Send the landlord text and keep a copy
- [ ] Optional: if your new job offers a retirement plan with an employer match, find out how to join. A match is effectively free money. That's next weekend's job if this one's already full.

Enjoy the coffee. You're setting yourself up well.
